summary: Year 3 children calculate with standard-unit measures: adding and subtracting lengths (m/cm/mm), masses (kg/g) and volumes/capacities (l/ml). The governing rule is 'same unit before you calculate': you only add or subtract measures expressed in the same unit, and the answer keeps that unit (250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml). Arithmetic stays within a single unit at this stage; systematic mm–cm–m conversion comes later, so mixed-unit sums are not yet expected. A number line / tape model makes combining (stacking) versus differencing (finding the gap) concrete, and every answer must carry its unit.
misconceptions: Adds or subtracts across different units as if they were the same number (2 m + 30 cm = 32).
Drops the unit from the answer (250 ml + 400 ml = 650).
Muddles compound units, e.g. reads 3 cm 5 mm as 35 or adds 3 + 5 — not yet knowing 10 mm = 1 cm.
Applies the wrong operation — adds when the problem asks for a difference, or vice versa.

activities.title: Measure-and-combine bench with a number line
steps: Measure two real quantities of the SAME kind — e.g. two lengths of ribbon in cm, or two beakers of juice in ml (250 ml and 400 ml), or two masses in g.

Combine the two measures on a number line / tape: place lengths end to end to read the total (e.g. 25 cm + 40 cm = 65 cm), or mark the two volumes along the scale to reach the total (250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml). Write the answer WITH its unit (65 cm; 650 ml).
Switch to a subtraction task: use the same number line to find the difference between the two measures as the gap between them.
Decide for each worded problem whether you are combining the amounts (stack them / mark to the total) or finding how much more one is than the other (find the gap).

Meet the mixed-unit case: a 2 m length and a 30 cm length. Try to total them and notice you cannot simply write 32 — line both up on one common scale (2 m lines up as 200 cm) and say what has to be true (same unit) before adding.
activities.insight: Adding measures means combining amounts and subtracting means finding a gap; a measurement answer is only meaningful with its unit; and you can only add or subtract measures that are in the same unit.

activities.title: Same-unit calculation check with targeted wrong-answer options
steps: Complete fill-in-the-blank sums within one unit, writing the unit in the answer (e.g. 250 ml + 400 ml = ___ ml).
Choose the correct result from options that include one that drops the unit and one that adds across units (e.g. for 2 m + 30 cm, recognise that '32' is wrong).
Explain in words why the across-unit option is wrong before moving on.
activities.insight: The same-unit rule and the unit-bearing answer can be stated explicitly and recognised in others' work, not just produced on the bench.

activities.title: Reference number-line diagram of a length addition
steps: Study a labelled number line / tape showing two lengths placed end to end and the total read off the scale.
Trace along the line to see where the first length ends and the second begins, and where the total sits.
Describe in your own words why the total is found by combining distances, and identify where the unit appears in the answer.
activities.insight: A worked tape/number-line picture shows the combining idea and anchors the vocabulary, as a reference to support the active measure-and-calculate work.

checkQuestion: Give real quantities to measure and combine: e.g. two lengths of ribbon and two beakers of water, plus a written problem ('250 ml + 400 ml = ?') and a deliberately mixed-unit one ('2 m + 30 cm = ?'). Say: 'Measure these and work out the totals and the difference.' Watch whether they keep like units together, carry the unit into the answer, and choose the right operation.
checkAnswer: The child adds/subtracts measures that are in the same unit, keeps the unit in the answer (650 ml; 7 cm), chooses the operation that fits the problem, and — faced with the mixed-unit item — recognises the units must match first rather than adding 2 + 30 to get 32.
